Microservices were practiced for a decade before they were named in 2012 and described in 2014 — and that 2014 description is the ruler every later ‘AI changed it’ claim will be measured against.

Nobody invented microservices on a given day. The habit of small programs that do one thing and talk through simple channels is as old as Unix. Amazon and Netflix practiced it under other names because their single big applications stopped scaling; a group of architects gave it the name in 2012; Lewis and Fowler described it in 2014; and by 2015 the same people were warning about its price. The chapter’s job is to fix the 2014 description as the ruler.

items.definition: One program, one deployment, one database — the shape microservices are contrasted with.
Service-oriented architecture: the 1990s–2000s idea of sharing logic and data through service interfaces; in enterprises it often arrived as SOAP and a central bus.
An XML-based protocol for calling services, heavy on formal contracts and tooling.
A central piece of middleware that routed, transformed, and applied rules to messages between applications — the ‘smart pipe’ microservices rejected.
Melvin Conway’s 1968 observation, now ‘Conway’s law’: a system’s structure copies the communication structure of the organization that builds it.
An application split only into a client and a database, with the logic in one or the other.
Assuming remote calls will fail and building timeouts, circuit breakers, and fallbacks in from the start.
The tool that made containers ordinary: a packaged, isolated process with everything it needs, portable from laptop to server.
Software that places, starts, restarts, and scales many containers across many machines (‘orchestration’).
The first service mesh (2016): a layer of proxies beside every service that handles retries, encryption, and routing.
One deployable unit whose internal boundaries are enforced in the code, so it could be split later.
Heroku’s 2011 rules for applications that run well on a platform: configuration in the environment, disposable processes, logs as streams.
Brewer’s 2000 statement that a distributed store cannot promise consistency, availability, and partition tolerance all at once.
Fielding’s 2000 web style: resources with addresses, manipulated through a small set of verbs.

runs.t: Microservices were a running practice for more than a decade before the industry had a stable name for them.
The word was argued over in 2011 and 2012 and fixed in public on 25 March 2014, when James Lewis and Martin Fowler published “Microservices” on martinfowler.com.
That article is the baseline for the rest of this research: any claim that AI changed the architecture has to say which part of that 2014 style actually moved.

blocks.text: The style is older than the word

runs.t: Fowler and Lewis said the roots go back at least to Unix: small programs, each doing one job, joined by simple pipes. Lewis’s March 2012 talk in Kraków was titled “Microservices — Java, the Unix Way.” The organizational idea is older still.
Melvin Conway wrote in 1968 that a system copies the communication structure of the organization that designs it.
That sentence later justified drawing service boundaries along business teams.

On 12 April 1996, Gartner analysts Roy Schulte and Yefim Natis described a “service oriented” architecture: shared logic and data, reached through interfaces, so many applications could use the same capability. Through the 2000s that idea often arrived in enterprises as
SOAP
, central governance, and an
enterprise service bus
that routed, transformed, and applied rules.
Lewis and Fowler wrote the 2014 article because “SOA” had come to mean too many incompatible things, and the systems they admired were a sharper variant: smart services, dull pipes.

In 1998, senior Amazon engineers wrote the Distributed Computing Manifesto. Werner Vogels published that memo in 2022. It separates presentation, business logic, and data, and it has clients reach data only through a service. In a 2006 interview for ACM Queue, Vogels said the
two-tier
monolith
had stopped scaling around 2001.
The rule they adopted was: encapsulate the data with the logic that uses it, allow no outside database access, and share no data between services.

A 2011 account by former Amazon engineer Steve Yegge describes a Jeff Bezos mandate, around 2002, that every team expose its data only through a network interface designed as if outsiders might call it. That memo is a retelling, so it is weaker evidence than Vogels. The public consequence is firmer: Amazon Web Services launched in 2006 by externalizing infrastructure Amazon had built for itself.

blocks.text: Netflix made the style famous at web scale

runs.t: Adrian Cockcroft later described a 2008 data-center outage that took Netflix down for several days, as streaming load was arriving on top of the DVD business. The decision was to leave data-center operations and rebuild for the cloud. He called the result “fine-grained
SOA
.” The customer-facing product was running in AWS by about the end of 2011.
The tools that leaked into the industry — Eureka, Hystrix, Zuul, and Chaos Monkey — are the public form of one 2014 characteristic: design for failure, because a remote call will fail.

In May 2011 a workshop of architects near Venice found they had been building the same style under different labels. Lewis presented it in March 2012 at the 33rd Degree conference in Kraków. Fred George was speaking about the same ideas around the same time. In May 2012 that group chose “microservices.”
Docker was shown at PyCon and open-sourced on 20 March 2013, which made a service a portable deployable unit.
Kubernetes

’s first commit is 6 June 2014. Eric Brewer announced the project at DockerCon on 10 June 2014. Kubernetes 1.0 and the Cloud Native Computing Foundation were announced together on 21 July 2015. Sam Newman’s Building Microservices (2015) became the practice manual.
Linkerd
(2016) and Istio (2017) then added a traffic layer — discovery, retries, and routing — because operating hundreds of services had become its own problem.

blocks.text: The same year as the boom, the cost was named

runs.t: On 13 May 2015 Fowler published “MicroservicePremium”: distribution adds complexity and risk, and teams that take it on before they need it get into trouble.
From 2015 through about 2021 the correction was monolith-first advice and the
modular monolith
. Many systems called microservices were one deployment unit sliced across the network, still sharing a database and a release train.

blocks.text: What the 2014 article fixed as the style

runs.t: Lewis and Fowler refused a formal definition.

They listed characteristics they kept seeing in the field. Most systems called microservices showed most of these, and the list is what later writers argued with. These nine characteristics are the baseline this research will test against AI.

rows: Characteristic
What it required
Services as components
Independently replaceable processes, reached by a remote call, rather than libraries linked into one executable.
Business capabilities
Boundaries follow the business, and teams are cross-functional. Conway’s Law (1968) is the cited reason.
Products, not projects
The team that builds a service keeps it. Amazon’s phrase was “you build it, you run it.”
Smart endpoints, dumb pipes
HTTP or a plain message bus. Routing and business rules stay in the service, away from an enterprise service bus.
Decentralized governance
Each service may choose its language and libraries. Shared tools are harvested from working code.
Decentralized data
Each service owns its data. Bounded contexts (Evans, 2003) and separate databases are the usual shape.
Infrastructure automation
Independent deployability only works with automated build and release.
Design for failure
Remote calls fail. Timeouts, circuit breakers, and isolation are part of the design.
Evolutionary design
Services can be split, replaced, or retired without a coordinated rewrite of the whole system.

runs.t: Source: James Lewis and Martin Fowler, “Microservices,” martinfowler.com, 25 March 2014.

blocks.text: Two lineages that predate the name

runs.t: A retail monolith that could not scale as a two-tier application. The remedy was service isolation: each capability owns its data and publishes an interface. By Vogels’s 2006 account, that move was already a decentralized services platform. Public AWS, from 2006, externalized infrastructure those teams had built for themselves.

A single Java application on Oracle, then a multi-day data-center failure as streaming load arrived. Cockcroft’s program was cloud-native decomposition, with the customer-facing product in AWS by about the end of 2011. Eureka, Hystrix, Zuul, and Chaos Monkey are the public tools of
design for failure
The style was a rejection of one central brain — the enterprise service bus — in favor of many smart services and dull pipes.
Any claim that AI changed microservice architecture has to say which of the nine 2014 characteristics moved: boundaries, ownership, pipes, data, deployment, or failure design.
This chapter stops before the AI wave. The next chapter records the architectures and design patterns of the style as it stood.

blocks.title: Read it again: three things to carry away

paragraphs.t: The practice is decades older than the name: the name is from 2012, the description from 25 March 2014.
Amazon and Netflix reached it by necessity — a monolith that stopped scaling, an outage that lasted days.
The nine characteristics of 2014 are the ruler; the 2015 ‘premium’ is the warning that travels with it.
